clue.text: First character to overturn attitude -of hare fanciers?

parts.note: the first character of the alphabet is A

indicators.note: overturning a word in an across clue means writing it from right to left

parts.note: an attitude is a pose struck by the body

explanation.surface: A reader puzzles over the leading figure whose stance offends people who keep hares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to overturn' turns POSE into ESOP. The definition is whimsical: the Greek fabulist told the tale of the hare and the tortoise, so he is the one 'of hare fancies'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek storyteller is famous for the fable of the boastful hare beaten by the slow tortoise.

clue.text: One is laid out at Kew from a right, well over stomach

definitions.text: One is laid out at Kew

parts.note: a bore is a well drilled for water; over places it above the next piece in a down clue
tum is a colloquial word for the stomach

explanation.surface: Directions to a spot in Kew Gardens, beginning from the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Kew Gardens in London is home to the Royal Botanic Gardens; 'over' means above in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree garden, a collection planted for study, is exactly what the botanic gardens at Kew contain.

clue.text: Unfortunate lapse, bit of a bloomer

indicators.note: an unfortunate word ends up in a bad state, so its letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A regrettable slip, something of a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' reads as a blunder, which matches 'lapse', but it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf-like part of the calyx forms part of a flower.

clue.text: Artist's bow-tie?

definitions.meaning: an artist is one who works in oils or watercolours; the 's reads as 'is'
a rope attached to the bow of a boat for tying it up

explanation.surface: Asking whether the artist's neckwear is a bow tie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bow-tie' reads as neckwear but is a tie at a boat's bow, the line used to moor it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes pictures in oils, and the mooring line fixed to a boat's front.

clue.text: Course from which you get back with a slice

parts.note: the rump is the hindquarters or back end of an animal
a steak is a thick slice of meat or fish

explanation.surface: A cryptic hint about a dinner course and what the butcher hands you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' is a dish served at a meal, not a race or a path; 'from which you get' just links the definition to the two cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut of beef from the hindquarters is served as the main dish of a meal.

clue.text: Bunter's form to change houses

definitions.meaning: Billy Bunter, the greedy schoolboy of Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories, is in the class of that name
to move home from one dwelling to another

explanation.surface: The fat schoolboy's class is moving house.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is a comic fat schoolboy in old British boys' stories; some English schools call a particular class the Remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A school class at Greyfriars, and to shift a household elsewhere.

clue.text: Those heard are sweet, said Keats — and fade away in Aegean Island?

definitions.text: Those heard are sweet, said Keats

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: Melos is a Greek island in the Aegean Sea
to die is to fade away

explanation.surface: Quoting Keats on sweet sounds, then wondering whether they vanish on a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn says 'Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter'; the Grecian theme carries on to the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's ode praises tunes that are heard as sweet, and those unheard as sweeter.

clue.text: Throttle left out — how odd!

indicators.note: out means the letter for left is removed

parts.note: to throttle someone is to strangle them

explanation.surface: Someone notices the throttle lever is missing and is surprised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throttle' looks like the engine control, but it is a verb meaning choke.
explanation.definitionFit: Peculiar and unusual are synonyms of each other in this sense.

clue.text: Orchid-growing perhaps (semi-toxic variety)

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the letters take another arrangement

explanation.surface: Raising orchids, which may be slightly poisonous, as a variety of hobby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' reads as a type of orchid, but it signals a new arrangement of SEMITOXIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Cultivating rare tropical plants is an example of a taste for the foreign and unusual.

clue.text: Equipment extremely tidy for the pool

parts.note: kit is equipment or gear

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Neat gear set out for the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pool' suggests swimming, but it is a pooled fund of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A pooled fund of stakes in a card game, or a shared fund for joint spending.

clue.text: Concerned with launching blimps at a resort

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, so these letters are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone's job is sending airships up at a seaside holiday town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town but is read as re-sort, rearranging BLIMPS AT A.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships are launched with a christening ceremony, and baptism is the church rite of naming and launching a new life.

clue.text: Place for retiring — or retiring to south, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters gathered may be arranged some other way
something retiring draws back, so the word or is read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A bedroom, or else a move to warmer parts on retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' turns OR into RO; with TO and S that gives ROTOS, and 'perhaps' asks for those letters rearranged. The setter plays on 'retiring' twice: going to bed, and drawing back.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds settle on a perch to sleep, so their nightly perch is where they go to bed.

clue.text: What makes blood thicker than water, specifically?

definitions.text: What makes blood thicker than water, specifically?

parts.words: What makes blood thicker than water, specifically?
parts.note: the proverb about family ties is read literally as a physics question about how heavy a liquid is compared with water

explanation.surface: Why family ties matter more than friendship, asked as a proverb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blood is thicker than water' means family comes first; 'specifically' points to specific gravity, the ratio of a substance's density to water's, and the first word puns on family relations.
explanation.definitionFit: The physics term for how dense a substance is compared with water is another name for specific gravity.

clue.text: Some of the chaps get blotto persistently

definitions.text: Some of the chaps get blotto persistently

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are used, a run lying inside them

explanation.surface: A remark that certain men regularly get blind drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines hard drinkers, while 'Some of' picks the six letters running across 'blotto persistently'.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual heavy drinkers are men who are regularly intoxicated.

clue.text: Our supine organisation is stingy

indicators.note: organisation means arranging, so the letters are set in a new order

explanation.surface: Our slack, lazy company is mean with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organisation' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it signals rearranging OURSUPINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being poverty-stricken or miserly both fit the sense of mean with money.

clue.text: "Then dreams he of another ——" (R. and J.)

definitions.text: "Then dreams he of another ——" (R. and J.)

parts.words: "Then dreams he of another ——" (R. and J.)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Mercutio's Queen Mab speech, where a sleeping parson dreams of a further church living

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Romeo and Juliet Mercutio describes Queen Mab tickling a parson's nose so that he dreams of another paid church post; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: In the speech the parson longs for a further church living, an ecclesiastical post that brings an income.

clue.text: See fourth in Derby having girth adjusted? It is a plant!

parts.note: to eye is to see or look at

indicators.note: the fourth letter in the word Derby is picked
adjusted means changed, so the letters of girth are rearranged

explanation.surface: Watch the fourth runner in the Derby, its saddle strap tightened.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is a famous English horse race at Epsom; a girth is the strap holding a saddle on. 'adjusted' turns GIRTH into RIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A small meadow flower once used to treat eye ailments, hence its name.

clue.text: Composer of sad organ pieces

indicators.note: broken into pieces, so the letters are scattered and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A composer who wrote melancholy organ pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pieces' reads as musical works, but it means bits, signalling an anagram of SADORGAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Enrique Granados was a Spanish composer, best known for the piano suite Goyescas.

clue.text: Many revs make small cars go

parts.note: the Mini is a small British car, so small cars are Minis
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Engines turning over fast get little cars moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revs' looks like engine revolutions to match the cars, but it is short for reverends: the clergy as a body.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of clergy collectively is a term for priests and ministers of religion.

clue.text: South American custom-built banger

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
usage is custom or habitual practice

explanation.surface: A made-to-order South American firework or old car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banger' is British slang for a sausage (and also a firework or old car); 'built' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a sausage, from its habit of bursting in the pan.

clue.text: Your head in Times puzzle, there is some difficulty of course

indicators.note: to puzzle is to confuse, so the letters are jumbled
the head of a word is its first letter, here the first letter of the word your

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The solver bent over the Times crossword is stuck, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Your head' gives Y, which goes with TIMES and is jumbled by 'puzzle'. 'of course' means on a golf course: an old rule where a ball blocks another's line to the hole.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, an obstruction is a ball lying between an opponent's ball and the hole, hence any obstacle.

clue.text: Filipino language to follow — it has no name

indicators.note: has no means the letter for name is taken out

parts.note: to tag along is to follow someone

explanation.surface: Learning the Philippine tongue as a follower, nameless.
explanation.definitionFit: The main language of the Philippines, the basis of the national tongue Filipino.

clue.text: A voiced sound heard in confession

indicators.note: heard means the phrase is pronounced, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a voiced sound made with the mouth open is a vowel; with a, a vowel

explanation.surface: A whispered sound overheard in the confessional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' tells you that 'a vowel' is said aloud, sounding like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An open admission or declaration is a frank statement of the truth.

clue.text: Latin-derived name for Chichester

parts.note: Chichester is not the cathedral city here but the yachtsman Sir Francis Chichester, who sailed alone around the world; the Latin roots mean going round and sailing

explanation.surface: Asking for the Roman name of the cathedral city of Chichester.
explanation.walkthrough: Chichester is a city in West Sussex with a Roman past, so the solver seeks a Latin town name; but Sir Francis Chichester sailed solo around the globe in 1966-67, and the answer is built from Latin circum (around) and navigare (sail).
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Chichester was a sailor who went right round the globe single-handed.

clue.text: Old Chester turned up after a century of being hollowed out

indicators.note: after puts the old city name behind the century letter

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means read from bottom to top

parts.note: Deva was the Roman name for Chester

explanation.surface: Old Chester dug up after a hundred years of excavation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' reverses DEVA, the Roman fort that became Chester, to AVED. 'of being' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has had its inside dug out is excavated or fallen in.

clue.text: Race, one of ten lost in Israel

definitions.meaning: a race in the sense of a people or clan

definitions.text: one of ten lost in Israel
definitions.meaning: the ten lost ... of Israel vanished from the Bible narrative after the Assyrian conquest

explanation.surface: A competition in which one of ten got lost in Israel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' reads as a contest, but it means a people.
explanation.definitionFit: A people or clan, and one of the ten lost divisions of ancient Israel.

clue.text: Bowed lady

definitions.meaning: a bowed instrument, played with a bow: one slightly larger than a violin
the heroine of Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, a lady disguised as a page

explanation.surface: A woman bending forward or curtsying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowed' reads as bent over, but it means played with a bow.
explanation.definitionFit: A stringed instrument played with a bow, and the shipwrecked heroine of Twelfth Night.

clue.text: Wooden pins of varying lengths go along nicely in Gateshead

parts.note: to do well is to make good progress
taken as written
read as Gate's head, the first letter of the word gate

explanation.surface: Wooden pegs cut to different sizes doing fine in a town on the Tyne.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town in north-east England opposite Newcastle; here it is split as 'Gate's head', its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lengths of round wooden rod used as joining pegs, cut to size for the job.

clue.text: Bad press in the face of being scattered

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: the face of a clock or meter is its dial

indicators.note: something bad is spoiled, so the word press is mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Negative reporting in the newspapers drives people apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad press' reads as one phrase meaning hostile coverage, but 'Bad' is the anagram signal working on the next word alone, and 'the face' means a clock face.
explanation.definitionFit: Spreading out over a wide area is the act of breaking up and going in different directions.

clue.text: Left after midnight for the county

indicators.note: after puts the departure word behind the midnight letter

parts.note: the middle of the word night is its middle letter, G
left in the sense of departed means went

explanation.surface: Someone departed after twelve at night, heading for a rural area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a direction, but it is the past tense of leave. Gwent is a county in south-east Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A former county in south-east Wales, bordering England.
